pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Grouping Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties." Non-statutory guidance expects pupils to "sort objects and materials into simple groups" and to explore and compare using the property vocabulary (hard/soft, shiny/dull, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, etc.).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." The clarification frames classifying as finding "patterns" — shared observable properties — across materials. DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." CCC: Patterns.

- **Operational details:** Move children from describing one material to comparing several and sorting them by a chosen property. Start with a single clear criterion (transparent vs opaque; waterproof vs absorbent) so groups are unambiguous, then compare two materials directly ('what is the same, what is different?'). Insist the child STATES the sorting rule and justifies each placement with a property word ('I put the window with the glass because you can see through both'). Crucially, re-sort the SAME set by a new property so children learn that grouping depends on the rule chosen, not on a fixed identity of the object. This is the first appearance of the compare-and-classify skill that recurs through states of matter, rocks and beyond.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can sort a set of materials by a chosen property, compare two materials naming a shared and a differing property, and explain a grouping decision in property words — and can re-group the same set by a different property when asked.
bestPractices: Begin with one clear either/or property (transparent vs opaque) so the sorting rule is unambiguous before introducing finer distinctions.
Require the child to name the sorting rule and justify each placement with a property word, making the reasoning explicit rather than intuitive.
Re-sort the same materials by a different property so children learn that groups depend on the chosen rule, not on a fixed property of the object — the core of the Patterns crosscutting concept.
Use direct pair comparison ('same/different') as a stepping stone from describing one material to grouping many.
Keep the sort hands-on with real materials and physical hoops/trays; concrete sorting is the KS1 route into classification.
Include ambiguous or multi-property items to prompt discussion ('could this go in either group? why?'), treating disagreement as reasoning practice.
keyRepresentations: Sorting hoops / trays labelled by a property (transparent | opaque)
A two-material compare frame: 'same' column and 'different' column
A regroupable set the child sorts, then re-sorts by a new property
A simple Carroll/Venn-style two-way mat for a later 'shiny AND hard' sort
Property-word tags the child attaches to each group to state the rule
commonMisconceptions: Believing a material has one fixed group, not realising the same set re-sorts differently when the property changes (a Patterns-concept hurdle).
Sorting by the object's identity or use (all the cups together) instead of by the stated physical property.
Grouping by irrelevant surface features (colour, size) rather than the chosen property.
Placing an item without a rule — grouping intuitively and being unable to justify it in property words.
Assuming a material can only ever be in one group, so an item that is both shiny and hard can't belong to two overlapping sorts.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds learning to compare and group everyday materials by simple physical properties. The core objective is that children sort a real set of materials by a stated property, justify each placement with a property word, and — crucially — re-sort the SAME set by a different property to discover that groups depend on the chosen rule, not on a fixed identity of the object. Activities centre on hands-on sorting with real materials; a drag-to-sort surface, a tap-to-reveal illustrated sort, and a short categorisation check are included as complementary supports with their limits noted.

activities.title: Sort real materials, then re-sort by a new rule
feedback: If the rule drifts mid-sort (starts by colour, slips to size or 'ones I like'), pause and have the child say their ONE rule aloud and hold it up, then re-run the sort against that fixed rule — the idea is fine, the procedure just needs anchoring.

If the child sorts by what objects are FOR ('the cup and jar go together because they hold things'), redirect to 'what is it MADE of / what is it LIKE to touch?'; if it persists, practise describing one material's properties before grouping.

If the child treats each material as having one permanent home and cannot re-sort, make the same object land in different groups in front of them — foil with the wood under 'see-through vs not see-through' (neither is see-through), foil with the fabric and sponge under 'bendy vs stiff' — so the group is seen to follow the chosen property.
Praise naming the rule and justifying placements with property words, not just getting items in the 'right' pile.
activities.rationale: Hands-on sorting of real materials and physical hoops/trays is the KS1 route into classification, and re-sorting the identical set by a new property makes the Patterns idea (groups depend on the chosen rule) enactable rather than told. Insisting the child states the rule and justifies with property words makes reasoning explicit.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties'; sort into simple groups.
NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; classifying = finding patterns of shared properties; CCC Patterns; DCI PS1.A.
Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Lay out a tray of real materials: wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric.
Choose ONE property and say the rule out loud before touching anything (e.g. 'see-through vs not see-through').
Sort every item into two hoops or trays, saying a property word for each placement ('I put the glass jar with the clear plastic toy because you can see through both').
Now sort the SAME items again, but pick a DIFFERENT property (e.g. bendy vs stiff, or hard vs softer). Notice which items move home.

Point out an item that changed groups and say why (e.g. 'the foil was with the wood for not see-through, but with the fabric and sponge for bendy'; the glass only leaves the plastic under 'hard' if the plastic toy is soft or squashy).

If you are ready, use two overlapping hoops labelled with two different properties (e.g. 'shiny' and 'hard') and put an item that has both, such as the metal key, in the overlap; an either/or pair like see-through vs not see-through or bendy vs stiff has no true overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: A group is not a fixed fact about an object; it depends on the property you choose to look at. The same material can belong with different partners under different rules.

activities.title: Same-and-different pair comparison
feedback: If the child names a use or feeling ('I like it') instead of a property, ask 'what is it like — hard or soft? shiny or dull? see-through or not?'
Accept any defensible property as long as it is a property of the material, and check the 'same' and 'different' entries actually match the two items.
activities.rationale: Direct pair comparison ('what is the same, what is different?') is a recommended stepping stone from describing one material to grouping many, and keeps the property vocabulary active.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties'; sort into simple groups.
learnerActions: Take just two materials at a time (e.g. glass jar and clear plastic toy; or wood block and metal key).
Say one property they SHARE ('both are hard' or 'you can see through both').
Say one property where they DIFFER ('the glass is see-through but the wood is not').
Record each in a 'same' column and a 'different' column, using property words.
Repeat with other pairs so comparing becomes a stepping stone into sorting a larger jumble.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing two materials by naming a shared and a differing property is the bridge from describing one material to grouping many.

activities.title: Read a finished sort and explain each placement (illustrated support)
feedback: Prompt the child to use a property word for each item, not just 'it goes there'.
Use the two arrangements to ask 'why did this one move?' so the rule-dependence is noticed, not just shown.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal illustrated sort can show a finished grouping and voice the property reasons, which reinforces vocabulary for pre-readers, and the second re-sorted arrangement targets the documented misconception that the same set cannot regroup under a new rule. Treated here as a support: it illustrates grouping but does not elicit the child's own sorting decisions, so pair it with the hands-on activity.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Look at a completed transparent/opaque grouping of pictured materials.
Tap or point to any item to hear or say the property reason it sits where it does ('this is here because you can see through it').
Then look at the same items shown re-sorted by a new rule (e.g. waterproof vs absorbent) and notice which pictures moved.
Say which item changed group and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Each group follows a property rule, and the same items can be arranged differently under a different rule — reinforcing the vocabulary and hinting at rule-dependence.

activities.title: Drag-to-sort bench with a swappable rule (optional interactive support)
feedback: For an unambiguous either/or sort, immediate right/wrong feedback can confirm whether a placement obeys the current rule; always have the child state the rule before sorting so feedback is about the reasoning.
Ambiguous or multi-property items are not errors — route them to the 'both'/overlap zone and treat them as a discussion prompt ('could this go in either group? why?') rather than marking them wrong.
When an item moves after the rule change, draw attention to it: 'last time the metal was with the wood — why is it with the glass now?'
activities.rationale: A drag-and-sort surface with live state and a re-sort control lets a child enact the rule change and watch the same items redistribute, which a static picture cannot do. Offered as one good vehicle, not the only way: real-material sorting delivers the same core experience with tactile handling.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Drag a jumble of pictured materials into two bins labelled 'transparent' and 'opaque' — glass and clear plastic to one side, wood and metal to the other — saying why each goes where.
Press a 'change the rule' control so the bins relabel to 'waterproof' and 'absorbent' and the items scatter, then sort the very SAME materials again.

Notice an item that genuinely changes partners — for example the metal key, which sat in the 'opaque' group with the wood but now joins the glass and plastic in the 'waterproof' group, while the wood (shown as bare, unvarnished wood, which slowly soaks up water) moves to 'absorbent'.

Use a 'both / not sure' zone for a borderline item, such as wood that soaks up water only slowly, and discuss it; for items that truly have two properties at once, use two non-opposite labels such as 'shiny' and 'hard' (for children ready to go further).
activities.intendedInsight: Switching the rule and watching the same set redistribute makes directly experienceable that groups depend on the chosen property.

activities.title: Quick categorisation and odd-one-out check
feedback: For odd-one-out, require the property reason, not just the choice.
This checks one sort at a time; follow any check with a live re-sort by a new rule to see whether the child understands rule-dependence.
activities.rationale: A categorisation step is itself a grouping task and scores cleanly; odd-one-out and compare-pair matching probe comparison. Used for assessment of applying a single rule, it does not by itself stage the re-sort realisation, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on activity.
learnerActions: Drag or place items into two property bins to show you can apply a single rule.
Answer an 'odd one out by property' question (which one does not belong, and which property makes it the odd one?).
Match a compare-pair: given two items, say the shared property.
For pre-readers, use pictures with spoken labels.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can demonstrate they sort by a single stated property and spot shared or differing properties.

constraints: Begin with one clear either/or property (transparent vs opaque) so the sorting rule is unambiguous before introducing finer distinctions.
Always require the child to name the sorting rule aloud and justify each placement with a property word — the reasoning must be explicit, not intuitive.
The re-sort of the SAME set by a new property is the central objective; do not substitute a single sort for it.

When demonstrating that an item changes partners under a new rule, choose a pair that actually separates under that rule (e.g. foil leaves the wood and joins the fabric and sponge under 'bendy vs stiff'; metal leaves the wood and joins the glass under 'waterproof' if the wood is bare, since bare wood soaks up some water but varnished or painted wood may not). Glass leaves the plastic and joins the metal under 'hard' only if the plastic item is soft or bendy, because a rigid plastic toy is also hard. Do not claim two items separate under a rule they both satisfy (glass and clear plastic are both transparent AND both waterproof, so they stay together under either).
Include ambiguous or multi-property items to prompt discussion ('could this go in either group? why?'), treating disagreement as reasoning practice rather than as a scoring error.

Illustrated tap-to-reveal and categorisation formats can reinforce vocabulary or check a single sort, but recognition and viewing do not elicit the child's own sorting decisions or the re-grouping experience; pair them with hands-on sorting.

A screen drag-to-sort surface and physical hoops with real materials offer different affordances (immediate feedback and easy rule-swapping vs tactile handling); either can carry the core experience, so do not treat one as universally necessary.
Watch the child sort rather than only asking about it, so shifting or object-based criteria that a verbal answer would hide are caught.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS 2-PS1-1 and the STEM Learning misconceptions page) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The original row asserted a static picture 'cannot' do the re-sort, that 3D 'adds no conceptual value', and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the manipulation. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts; softened here to narrow affordance/limit statements. A fixed illustration can still teach vocabulary, and different media offer different experiences.
The original claimed re-sorting 'directly' produces the moment of insight. Retained as a strong pedagogical aim, not as a guaranteed outcome.
The worked justification example was adapted from the original 'window with the glass' to 'glass jar with the clear plastic toy' so it matches the stated material tray; meaning is unchanged.

Corrected a factual slip in the drag-to-sort example: the original recommendation claimed glass, grouped with the plastic under 'see-through', 'lands in a different place' under 'waterproof vs absorbent'. Glass and clear plastic are both waterproof and would stay together; the example was changed to the metal key moving between groups. The clean glass-separates-from-plastic contrast remains tied to the hard/soft rule.

Classifying a rigid clear plastic toy as 'softer' than glass is a relative KS1 comparison implied by the original's 'glass with metal under hard' example; phrased as a relative comparison rather than an absolute category.

probeDeeper: Could this glass jar go in the OTHER group if we picked a different rule? Which rule would move it?
Why did you put these two together — what is the same about them?
I'm going to move the foil into the other group — is that allowed under YOUR rule, or not?
If your rule is 'bendy', where does the sponge go — and how did you check whether it bends?
assess.correctAnswer: Sorts consistently by a single stated property (e.g. see-through vs not), names the rule, then re-sorts the identical set by a different property (e.g. bendy vs stiff) — showing that the groups depend on the property chosen, not on fixed identities of the materials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Criterion drifts mid-sort — starts grouping by colour, then quietly switches to size or 'ones I like', without noticing the rule changed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: 'Say your ONE rule out loud first', write/hold it up, then re-run the sort against that fixed rule. The concept is intact; the procedure needs anchoring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finished groups don't obey any single rule; items placed early and late follow different logics.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by object type or use rather than material property — 'the cup and the jar go together because they hold things'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to 'what is it MADE of / what is it LIKE to touch?'; if it persists, reteach the property-describing step before grouping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groups reflect what the objects are FOR, not a material property; property words are absent from the reasoning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Each material has one permanent group — 'glass is a see-through thing, that's where it goes' — so the child cannot re-sort the same set under a new rule.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the same object land in different groups under different rules on the table in front of them (glass with plastic under 'see-through', glass with metal under 'hard') so groups are seen to follow the chosen property.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the second sort, struggles or refuses; tries to reproduce the first grouping.

responseLevels.gap: Groups by vague, shifting or like/dislike reasons, or by what objects are used for; cannot state a rule.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by a chosen property with a clear stated rule AND re-sorts the identical set under a different property, articulating that the groups depend on the property chosen.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts consistently by one property and names the rule, but cannot re-group the SAME set by a new property — treats each material's group as fixed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a tray of materials (wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric). Say: 'Sort these into two groups using ONE property you choose, and tell me your rule.' Watch them do it. Then: 'Now sort the SAME things again, but pick a DIFFERENT property this time.' Watch whether they can re-group the identical set.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The re-sort is the tell. A child who can only place each material in one 'correct' home cannot re-group the same set; a child who understands grouping-by-property applies one consistent rule, names it, and cheerfully reshuffles the SAME items under a new rule. Watching (not asking about) the sort catches shifting or object-based criteria a verbal answer would hide.
